topic: dressing a floor loom for weaving, from winding the warp to tying on

provenance.author: glowny-en-d
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is warp arithmetic (ends, heddles, bouts, dents, timings) with closed task questions, base is a dialogue about dressing an inherited loom without slack bands. Grounded external referent: the warp beam, introduced in turn 0 (it takes the warp and carries it through the whole job) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion.

a: Here is the warp sheet for the floor loom, and the figures need working through in order.
The cloth is planned at twenty-four inches wide with a sett of twelve ends to the inch.
The warp length is eight yards for every end, with loom waste already counted inside.
The draft is a straight draw across four shafts, taking the ends in strict rotation.
How many warp ends does the sheet call for at that width and sett?
base: I have moved my grandmother's floor loom into the spare room and I want to dress it properly.
The warp is wound and chained, and the next step is getting it onto the loom.
The back beam takes the warp first, and every guide I read treats that winding as the make-or-break stage.
My last attempt on a smaller loom ended with loose bands of thread at one edge.
What actually causes those slack bands, and how do I stop them this time?

a: Twenty-four inches at twelve ends to the inch calls for two hundred eighty-eight ends.
A straight draw over four shafts puts seventy-two ends on every shaft.
Each end runs eight yards, so the warp holds two thousand three hundred four yards of thread.
A twelve dent reed at one end per dent uses two hundred eighty-eight dents exactly.
Does the two hundred eighty-eight match the end count printed on the warp sheet?
base: Slack bands nearly always come from uneven pull while the warp is being wound on.
Wind with firm, even weight on the whole chain, and stop often to shake the threads straight.
Lay stout paper between every layer, because bare layers let threads bite down into each other.
Keep the beam turning slowly and steadily rather than in quick pulls between pauses.
Do you have a second pair of hands to hold the chain while you wind?

a: Now divide the warp into bouts for winding, with forty-eight ends in every bout.
List how many full bouts that makes and whether any ends are left over.
Then give the count of heddles needed on each shaft for the straight draw.
The heddle boxes hold eighty heddles per shaft as they stand on the loom.
How many bouts of forty-eight come out of two hundred eighty-eight ends?
base: My neighbour can hold the chain on Saturday, so the winding is covered.
The beam on this loom is wide enough that the warp spreads without crowding.
I kept the cross tied at both ends of the chain, and the lease sticks are in.
The raddle sits on the back rail with the warp spread to its marked width.
Should the lease sticks stay in while the warp winds on, or come out first?

a: Two hundred eighty-eight ends divide into six full bouts of forty-eight with none left over.
Each shaft needs seventy-two heddles, which sits inside the eighty already on the loom.
The margin is eight spare heddles on every shaft before any are moved across.
Across the four shafts the draw uses two hundred eighty-eight heddles in total.
Do the six bouts and the heddle margins agree with the loom as it stands?
base: Leave the lease sticks in while you wind, because they comb the threads into order.
Tie them loosely to the back rail so they ride along without pinching the warp.
Once the beam carries the whole warp, move the sticks forward for threading.
Thread the heddles in your draft order, and check every group of four before moving on.
Which draft are you threading, a plain straight draw or something with a pattern repeat?

a: One correction before the winding starts, because the cloth width was changed last night.
The cloth is now twenty-six inches wide at the same twelve ends to the inch.
Recalculate the end count, the heddles per shaft and the total warp yardage.
Keep the bout size at forty-eight ends and report any remainder this time.
What does the end count become at twenty-six inches and twelve to the inch?
base: The plan is a straight draw over four shafts, nothing fancy for a first project.
I must correct one figure from before, because I recounted the ends this morning.
The warp holds three hundred twelve ends, not two hundred eighty-eight as I first said.
The beam took the full chain without trouble, and the layers look flat and tight.
Does the higher count change how I spread the ends across the raddle spaces?

a: Twenty-six inches at twelve to the inch calls for three hundred twelve ends.
Each shaft now needs seventy-eight heddles, still inside the eighty on the loom.
The warp yardage rises to two thousand four hundred ninety-six yards at eight yards an end.
Three hundred twelve ends make six full bouts of forty-eight with twenty-four left over.
Should the twenty-four spare ends wind as a seventh short bout on the sheet?
base: The raddle spreading changes only a little, with a few more ends in each space.
Divide the three hundred twelve ends evenly, and keep the edges slightly fuller than the middle.
The threading will take longer, so break it into sittings of about eighty ends.
Rest your eyes between sittings, because threading mistakes hide until the first inches are woven.
Have you counted your heddles, since each shaft must carry its share of the ends?

a: Yes, enter the seventh short bout and then move on to the reed figures.
The reed is a twelve dent, sleyed at one end through every dent across the width.
Give the dents used, the dents empty on a thirty inch reed, and the sleying time.
Sleying runs at four ends a minute once the reed hook finds its rhythm.
How many dents stay empty when three hundred twelve ends fill a thirty inch reed?
base: Each shaft carries about ninety heddles, so there is room to spare on all four.
I threaded the first eighty ends last night and found one crossed pair straight away.
Fixing the crossed pair meant rethreading a dozen ends, which taught me to check often.
The reed is a twelve dent, and the plan puts one end through each dent.
How tight should the tie-on be before I start looking at the tension band by band?

a: A thirty inch reed at twelve dents to the inch carries three hundred sixty dents in all.
Three hundred twelve ends fill three hundred twelve dents, leaving forty-eight dents empty.
Split evenly between the sides, that parks twenty-four empty dents at each edge of the web.
At four ends a minute the sleying takes seventy-eight minutes of steady work.
Is the seventy-eight minute figure the one that goes into the plan for the evening?
base: Tie on in small bundles with even firmness, and leave the knots easy to open.
Snug is enough at first, because you will tighten everything again after the first inspection.
Press a flat palm across the warp and feel for bands that give more than their neighbours.
Retie only the slack bundles, then bring the whole warp up to working tightness together.
Can you weave a few inches of scrap yarn first to settle the threads?

a: Now lay out the dressing in four sessions, with one task given to each session.
Session one is winding the bouts, and session two is beaming the warp.
Session three is threading the heddles, and session four is sleying and tying on.
Threading runs at three ends a minute, and the count is three hundred twelve ends.
That pace puts the threading session at one hundred four minutes of quiet work.
base: I have a cone of rough cotton that will do for the first scrap inches.
The plan for the weekend is winding on Saturday and threading across two evenings after.
Tying on and the scrap inches can wait for the following weekend without any rush.
The spare room smells of wood and wool now, which makes the work feel real.
My grandmother would laugh to see her loom taking over my house at last.

a: One hundred four minutes of threading is one hour and forty-four minutes at that pace.
Winding the seven bouts runs about ninety minutes with the swift and cone set up.
Beaming takes about an hour with a second pair of hands on the chain.
Sleying and tying on together come to roughly two hours at the measured rates.
The four sessions total close to six and a half hours from first bout to final knot.
base: That schedule is sensible, and the two threading evenings will go faster than you fear.
Keep a card by the loom and tick off every group of ends as it is threaded.
Note the tie-on date on the same card, along with the count and the draft.
Records like that turn the next warp from an experiment into a routine.
A well-dressed loom rewards every hour you have spent crawling around it this month.
